# A municipal report: Paranaguá {#sec-relatorio-paranagua}

Before automating a report for many cases (@sec-m5-parametrizados), you need a
report that works for **one** case. This chapter is that report, for Paranaguá (PR),
home of Paraná's main port: a short diagnosis of the municipality's territory, population and
economy, and of the coastal shipping that passes through it.

It brings together packages from several modules: `geobr` and `censobr` (@sec-m2-bases) for the territory and the
Census, `sidrar` for IBGE's series, `dplyr` and `ggplot2` for everything else. No number in the
text is typed in: they all come from the code, and that is why the same text works for another municipality.

::: {.callout-note}
## Downloads on the first run

`censobr` downloads the 2022 Census for the whole country, in Parquet, and stores it on your computer: about
200 MB the first time (most of it is the persons table, with colour or race), and nothing on
later runs. `geobr` also stores the boundaries. `sidrar` queries IBGE's API on each
run and needs an internet connection.
:::

## The municipality in two variables

```{r}
#| message: false
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

municipio <- "Paranaguá"
uf        <- "PR"

# the IBGE code: the key that links geobr, censobr and SIDRA
codigo <- geobr::lookup_muni(name_muni = municipio, year = 2022) |>
  dplyr::filter(abbrev_state == uf) |>
  dplyr::pull(code_muni)

codigo
```

The rest of the chapter uses only `municipio`, `uf` and `codigo`. The name and the state appear only
once, in this block. It is this discipline that, in the next chapter, turns the report into a template
for any municipality: just change this block.

## Territory

```{r}
limite  <- geobr::read_municipality(code_muni = codigo, year = 2022, showProgress = FALSE)
setores <- geobr::read_census_tract(code_tract = codigo, year = 2022, simplified = FALSE,
                                    showProgress = FALSE)

area_km2 <- as.numeric(sf::st_area(limite)) / 1e6
```

```{r}
# population and status (urban or rural) of each tract, from the 2022 Census
basico <- censobr::read_tracts(year = 2022, dataset = "Basico", as_data_frame = FALSE,
                               showProgress = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::filter(code_muni == codigo) |>
  dplyr::select(code_tract, situacao, populacao = V0001) |>
  dplyr::collect() |>
  # tracts without a status are bodies of water (bays, wide rivers), with no residents
  dplyr::mutate(situacao = dplyr::coalesce(situacao, "Water body"))

setores <- setores |>
  dplyr::left_join(basico, by = "code_tract") |>
  dplyr::mutate(area_setor = as.numeric(sf::st_area(geometry)) / 1e6)   # km²

pct_urbano <- with(setores, 100 * sum(area_setor[situacao == "Urbana"]) / sum(area_setor))
```

`r municipio` covers `r format(round(area_km2), big.mark = ",")` km², divided into
`r format(nrow(setores), big.mark = ",")` census tracts. The urban tracts occupy
`r format(round(pct_urbano, 1))`% of the municipality's area.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pgua-territorio
#| fig-cap: "Census tracts by status (2022 Census)"
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(setores) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = situacao), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_sf(data = limite, fill = NA, colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Urbana = "#1a5b8a", Rural = "#c9d6b3",
                               "Water body" = "#d6e6f2"),
                    labels = c(Urbana = "Urban", Rural = "Rural", "Water body" = "Water body"),
                    name = NULL) +
  theme_void()
```

## Population: censuses and estimates

SIDRA has the census population and the annual estimates IBGE publishes between them:

```{r}
#| message: false
censo_2010 <- sidrar::get_sidra(x = 1378, variable = 93, geo = "City",
                                geo.filter = list("City" = codigo),
                                classific = "c2", category = list(0))   # c2 = sex; 0 = total
censo_2022 <- sidrar::get_sidra(x = 4709, variable = 93, geo = "City",
                                geo.filter = list("City" = codigo))
estimativas <- sidrar::get_sidra(x = 6579, variable = 9324, period = "all", geo = "City",
                                 geo.filter = list("City" = codigo))

populacao <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  Census   = dplyr::bind_rows(censo_2010, censo_2022),
  Estimate = estimativas,
  .id = "fonte"
) |>
  dplyr::transmute(fonte, ano = as.integer(Ano), populacao = Valor)

pop_2022 <- populacao$populacao[populacao$fonte == "Census" & populacao$ano == 2022]
ultima   <- dplyr::slice_max(dplyr::filter(populacao, fonte == "Estimate"), ano)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pgua-populacao
#| fig-cap: "Resident population: IBGE censuses and estimates"
#| fig-height: 3.4
ggplot(populacao, aes(ano, populacao / 1000, colour = fonte)) +
  geom_line(data = dplyr::filter(populacao, fonte == "Estimate"), linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(size = fonte)) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(Census = 3, Estimate = 1.2), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Census = "#b3402a", Estimate = "#1a5b8a"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Thousand inhabitants") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

The 2022 Census counted `r format(pop_2022, big.mark = ",")` inhabitants; the most recent estimate,
for `r ultima$ano`, is `r format(ultima$populacao, big.mark = ",")`. Notice the difference between the
2021 estimate and the 2022 Census: a decade's estimates are projected from the
previous census and, when the new census arrives, the series is corrected. That is why the report uses the
census as the reference and says where each number comes from.

## Economy: GDP

```{r}
#| message: false
pib <- sidrar::get_sidra(x = 5938, variable = 37, period = "all", geo = "City",
                         geo.filter = list("City" = codigo)) |>
  dplyr::transmute(ano = as.integer(Ano), pib_bi = Valor / 1e6)   # thousand reais -> billions

pib_2022 <- pib$pib_bi[pib$ano == 2022]
pib_per_capita <- pib_2022 * 1e9 / pop_2022
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pgua-pib
#| fig-cap: "Municipal GDP at current prices (IBGE)"
#| fig-height: 3.2
ggplot(pib, aes(ano, pib_bi)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1a5b8a") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "R$ billion, current") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

In 2022, the GDP of `r municipio` was R$ `r format(round(pib_2022, 1))`
billion, or R$ `r format(round(pib_per_capita, -2), big.mark = ",")` per inhabitant. In
port municipalities, GDP per capita tends to reflect the value passing through the port more
than the income of the people who live there; income is two sections further on.

## Population across the territory

```{r}
setores <- dplyr::mutate(setores, densidade = populacao / area_setor)   # inhab/km²
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pgua-densidade
#| fig-cap: "Population density by census tract (2022 Census)"
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(setores) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = densidade), colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = limite, fill = NA, colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10", labels = scales::label_number(accuracy = 1, big.mark = ","),
                       name = "inhab/km²", na.value = "grey90") +
  theme_void()
```

## Income and colour or race

The 2022 Census publishes, by tract, the average income of household heads and the
population by colour or race:

```{r}
renda <- censobr::read_tracts(year = 2022, dataset = "ResponsavelRenda", as_data_frame = FALSE,
                              showProgress = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::filter(code_muni == codigo) |>
  dplyr::select(code_tract, renda = V06004) |>    # average income of household heads (R$)
  dplyr::collect()

cor <- censobr::read_tracts(year = 2022, dataset = "Pessoas", as_data_frame = FALSE,
                            showProgress = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::filter(code_muni == codigo) |>
  dplyr::select(code_tract, White = raca_V01317, Black = raca_V01318, Asian = raca_V01319,
                Brown = raca_V01320, Indigenous = raca_V01321) |>
  dplyr::collect()

setores <- setores |>
  dplyr::left_join(renda, by = "code_tract")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pgua-renda
#| fig-cap: "Average monthly income of household heads (2022 Census)"
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(setores) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = renda), colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = limite, fill = NA, colour = "grey20", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "YlGnBu", direction = 1, na.value = "grey90",
                       labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",", prefix = "R$ "),
                       name = NULL) +
  theme_void()
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pgua-cor
#| fig-cap: "Population by colour or race (2022 Census)"
#| fig-height: 2.6
por_cor <- cor |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-code_tract, names_to = "cor", values_to = "pessoas") |>
  dplyr::summarise(pessoas = sum(pessoas, na.rm = TRUE), .by = cor) |>
  dplyr::mutate(pct = 100 * pessoas / sum(pessoas))

ggplot(por_cor, aes(pct, reorder(cor, pct))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#1a5b8a") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(format(round(pct, 1)), "%")),
            hjust = -0.15, size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(x = "% of the population", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

## Coastal shipping

ANTAQ's coastal shipping throughput, in tonne-kilometres (TKU), seen from the
municipality: what leaves it (**outbound**) and what arrives (**inbound**).

```{r}
colunas <- c("ano", "perfil", "sh2",
             "pais_origem", "uf_origem", "cidade_origem", "instalacao_origem",
             "pais_destino", "uf_destino", "cidade_destino", "instalacao_destino",
             "tku")

cabotagem <- readxl::read_excel("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx", na = c("", "-"))
names(cabotagem) <- colunas

cabotagem <- cabotagem |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.character), stringr::str_squish)) |>
  dplyr::filter(tku > 0)

# each link that touches the municipality, with the direction and the municipality at the other end
fluxos <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  Outbound = cabotagem |>
    dplyr::filter(cidade_origem == municipio, uf_origem == uf) |>
    dplyr::mutate(parceiro = cidade_destino, uf_parceiro = uf_destino),
  Inbound = cabotagem |>
    dplyr::filter(cidade_destino == municipio, uf_destino == uf) |>
    dplyr::mutate(parceiro = cidade_origem, uf_parceiro = uf_origem),
  .id = "sentido"
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(parceiro = dplyr::if_else(is.na(parceiro), "EEZ/Platform",
                                          paste0(parceiro, " (", uf_parceiro, ")")))

resumo <- fluxos |>
  dplyr::summarise(ligacoes = dplyr::n(), tku_bi = sum(tku) / 1e9,
                   parceiros = dplyr::n_distinct(parceiro), .by = sentido)

resumo |> knitr::kable(digits = 2,
                       col.names = c("Direction", "Links", "TKU (billion t·km)",
                                                  "Partner municipalities"))
```

In `r cabotagem$ano[1]`, coastal shipping links with origin or destination in `r municipio`
added up to `r format(round(sum(resumo$tku_bi), 1))` billion t·km.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pgua-perfil
#| fig-cap: "TKU by cargo profile and direction"
#| fig-height: 2.8
fluxos |>
  dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku) / 1e9, .by = c(sentido, perfil)) |>
  ggplot(aes(tku_bi, reorder(perfil, tku_bi), fill = sentido)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Outbound = "#1a5b8a", Inbound = "#b3402a"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "TKU (billion t·km)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pgua-parceiros
#| fig-cap: "Main partner municipalities in coastal shipping"
#| fig-height: 3.4
fluxos |>
  dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku) / 1e9, .by = c(parceiro, sentido)) |>
  dplyr::filter(parceiro %in% (dplyr::count(fluxos, parceiro, wt = tku, sort = TRUE) |>
                                 dplyr::slice_head(n = 8) |> dplyr::pull(parceiro))) |>
  ggplot(aes(tku_bi, reorder(parceiro, tku_bi, sum), fill = sentido)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Outbound = "#1a5b8a", Inbound = "#b3402a"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "TKU (billion t·km)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

## From report to template

This chapter is already a complete report, and it works for one municipality. To produce it for the
five municipalities with the most coastal shipping in the country, the temptation is to copy the file five times and
replace "Paranaguá" by hand. The next chapter shows the better way: turn the first
block into **parameters** and render the same file five times.
